stem: When teaching mealtime infection prevention after transplantation, which hand-hygiene step aligns with standard references?

options.text: Wash hands before and after eating
Hand-washing is needed only after meals, not before
Eating never requires hand-washing at home
Mealtime hand hygiene applies only to pediatric recipients

explanation.rationale_correct: Recipient hand-hygiene teaching includes washing hands before and after eating, along with washing before preparing meals and after bathroom use or secretions contact.

rationale_incorrect.B: Hand-washing is recommended both before and after eating rather than only afterward.
rationale_incorrect.C: Home mealtime hand hygiene is specifically recommended rather than omitted.
rationale_incorrect.D: Mealtime hand-washing guidance applies to all recipients, not pediatric recipients alone.

primary_anchor.section: Ch. 3, Patient Education → e. Infection prevention → i. Hand hygiene

references.citation: Core Curriculum for Transplant Nurses, 2nd ed. (Cupples et al., 2016).
references.locator: Ch. 3 → e. Infection prevention → i. Hand hygiene (wash hands before and after eating); PDF p. 115 (repo file-page index; printed margin may differ).

notes: Source-first item. Mealtime hand-hygiene angle distinct from meal-preparation timing (cctc-1158) and general best-practice hand-washing (cctc-1019); anchor verified on Cupples p. 115.

stem: When reinforcing home infection-prevention teaching, which hand-hygiene step aligns with standard references after handling potentially contaminated household items?

options.text: Wash hands after touching any items that may have come in contact with feces
Fecal-contact items never require hand-washing if gloves were briefly used
Only hospital staff must wash hands after fecal exposure
Household fecal-contact items pose no infection risk to recipients

explanation.rationale_correct: Hand-hygiene teaching includes washing after touching any items that may have come in contact with feces, whether human or animal, along with washing after animals, soil, and secretions.

rationale_incorrect.B: Hand-washing after fecal-contact items is specifically recommended rather than being optional after brief glove use.
rationale_incorrect.C: Recipients themselves should wash hands after such exposures.
rationale_incorrect.D: Fecal-contact items are among exposures that warrant hand hygiene.

primary_anchor.section: Ch. 3, Patient Education → e. Infection prevention → i. Hand hygiene
primary_anchor.quote_hint: After touching any items that may have come in contact with feces (human or animal)

references.locator: Ch. 3 → e. Infection prevention → i. Hand hygiene (wash after items contacting feces); PDF p. 115 (repo file-page index; printed margin may differ).

stem: A transplant recipient with a household dog asks about infection prevention after routine pet contact. Which teaching point aligns with standard animal-safety references?

options.text: Follow strict hand hygiene guidelines after contact
Hand hygiene after pet contact is unnecessary for immunosuppressed recipients
Pet contact requires permanent removal of all household animals
Only veterinary staff need hand hygiene after animal contact

explanation.rationale_correct: Animal-safety teaching includes following strict hand hygiene guidelines after contact with pets, along with keeping pets immunized, avoiding animals with diarrhea, and postponing new pets until immunosuppression is more stable.

rationale_incorrect.B: Hand hygiene after pet contact is specifically recommended rather than omitted.
rationale_incorrect.C: Routine pet ownership may continue with precautions rather than requiring permanent removal of all animals.
rationale_incorrect.D: Recipients themselves should follow hand hygiene after contact rather than delegating it to veterinary staff alone.

primary_anchor.section: Ch. 3, Patient Education → e. Infection prevention → v. Animal safety
primary_anchor.quote_hint: Follow strict hand hygiene guidelines after contact

references.citation: Core Curriculum for Transplant Nurses, 2nd ed. (Cupples et al., 2016).
references.locator: Ch. 3 → e. Infection prevention → v. Animal safety (strict hand hygiene after pet contact); PDF p. 116 (repo file-page index; printed margin may differ).

notes: Source-first item. Post-contact hand-hygiene after pets angle distinct from animal-contact hand-washing on p. 115 (cctc-1156) and keep-pets-immunized teaching (cctc-1102); anchor verified on Cupples p. 116.

stem: A coordinator is updating mealtime and household infection-prevention teaching. Evaluate the following statements:

elements.text: Recipients should wash hands before and after eating.
Recipients should wash hands after touching items that may have contacted feces.
Recipients should follow strict hand hygiene guidelines after pet contact.
Hand-washing before meals is unnecessary if food will be cooked.

explanation.rationale_correct: Mealtime hand-washing, hand hygiene after fecal-contact items, and strict hand hygiene after pet contact are supported. Statement IV is false because hand-washing before and after eating is specifically recommended regardless of cooking.

rationale_incorrect.A: Statement III is also true—strict hand hygiene after pet contact is recommended.
rationale_incorrect.C: Statement I is also true; statement IV is false.
rationale_incorrect.D: Statement IV is false because mealtime hand-washing remains recommended.

primary_anchor.section: Ch. 3, Patient Education → e. Infection prevention → i. Hand hygiene and v. Animal safety
primary_anchor.quote_hint: Before and after eating … items that may have come in contact with feces … Follow strict hand hygiene guidelines after contact
